paraphrase: At the Vulture Peak the Buddha, after teaching the 'Immeasurable Meanings', enters samādhi; flowers rain, the earth shakes in six ways and a ray from the tuft between his brows lights up eighteen thousand worlds to the east, showing their beings, buddhas and stūpas. Maitreya asks why; Mañjuśrī recalls that the past buddha Candrasūryapradīpa showed the same sign before teaching the Lotus.

paraphrase: Whoever keeps, reads, recites, explains or copies even one verse of this sūtra, or honors it, is a messenger of the Tathāgata; where it is kept a stūpa should be built, needing no relics, for the Tathāgata's whole body is there. The preacher should enter the Tathāgata's room (compassion), wear his robe (patience) and sit on his seat (the emptiness of all dharmas).

paraphrase: A jewelled stūpa rises from the earth containing the extinct buddha Prabhūtaratna, who vowed to appear wherever the Lotus is taught; Śākyamuni gathers his emanation-buddhas from the ten directions, opens the stūpa and sits beside Prabhūtaratna, and the assembly is raised into the air.

paraphrase: Devadatta was, in a past life, the seer who taught the Buddha the Lotus, and he is predicted to become the buddha Devarāja.
notes: Reference from the unit author's knowledge at chapter level; passage not read in a local text in this phase. Chapter 12 in Kumārajīva (added after his translation); part of Skt ch. 11.

paraphrase: The eight-year-old daughter of the nāga king Sāgara, whom Mañjuśrī taught in the sea, is declared able to awaken quickly; Śāriputra objects that a woman's body cannot attain buddhahood. She gives the Buddha a jewel and, before the whole assembly, her female organ vanishes, a male one appears, she is a bodhisattva, goes south to the world Vimalā and there appears as a buddha teaching the dharma.

paraphrase: When bodhisattvas from other worlds offer to protect the sūtra, the Buddha declines: countless bodhisattvas rise from the earth beneath, whom he says he has taught since his awakening; Maitreya asks how, in forty-odd years, he could have taught so many.

paraphrase: The Tathāgata did not first awaken at Gayā: it is countless hundreds of thousands of myriads of koṭis of aeons since he awakened; his lifespan is immeasurable, he always abides, and he appears to enter nirvāṇa as a skillful means so that beings will not become complacent. Like a physician whose poisoned sons refuse the antidote until he sends word that he has died abroad — then they take it and recover — he is not guilty of lying.

paraphrase: The merit of the fiftieth person who, hearing the sūtra passed on from one to another, rejoices in it, exceeds that of giving every pleasure to all beings of four hundred myriad koṭis of worlds.

paraphrase: The buddhas appear in the world for one great purpose only: to open beings to the Tathāgata's knowledge and vision, to show it, to make them awaken to it and to make them enter its path. The buddhas' 'intentional speech' (saṃdhābhāṣya) is hard to understand; the dharma is beyond reasoning, known only to Tathāgatas.

paraphrase: The Buddha teaches the dharma to beings with reference to one vehicle only, the buddha-vehicle ending in all-knowledge; there is no second or third vehicle anywhere in the ten directions. When buddhas appear in times of the five turbidities — of the aeon, of beings, of defilements, of views, of lifespan — they teach that one buddha-vehicle by skillful means as three vehicles.

paraphrase: Those who in the past made offerings to buddhas' relics, built stūpas even of sand in play, made images even with a fingernail, offered a single flower or said 'namo buddhāya' once with distracted mind — all have attained, or will attain, the buddha-way.

paraphrase: The bodhisattva Sadāparibhūta (Never-Disparaging) approached every monk, nun and layperson and said: 'I do not disparage you; you are not disparaged, for you will all practice the bodhisattva way and become buddhas'; though they beat him with sticks and stones he kept saying it; he was a past life of Śākyamuni.

paraphrase: Whoever in fire, flood, storm, among robbers or at the executioner's sword, in chains, or beset by lust, anger and delusion calls single-mindedly on the name of Avalokiteśvara is freed at once; to those who wish for sons or daughters he grants them; he appears in whatever form — buddha, pratyekabuddha, śrāvaka, Brahmā, Indra, king, merchant, monk, woman, boy or girl — will liberate each being.

paraphrase: Samantabhadra vows that in the last age he will come on his six-tusked white elephant to protect and teach those who recite, study and copy the Lotus, appearing to them in visions and giving them dhāraṇīs; whoever keeps it has seen Śākyamuni.

paraphrase: The parable of the burning house: a rich man's old house catches fire while his children play inside, heedless; he lures them out by promising goat-, deer- and ox-carts they love, and when they are out gives each the same great, jewelled ox-cart. So the Tathāgata, father of the world, draws beings from the burning house of the three realms by the three vehicles and gives them all the one great vehicle — and is not guilty of falsehood.

paraphrase: The parable of the lost son, told by the great disciples: a son who ran away lives as a poor laborer; his rich father recognizes him but, knowing his low self-esteem, hires him for menial work and raises him gradually until at death he declares him heir. The disciples were content with a day's wage of nirvāṇa; the Buddha by skillful means led them to the inheritance of buddhahood.

paraphrase: The parable of the medicinal herbs: one cloud rains the same rain on all plants, which each take it according to their kind; so the Tathāgata's teaching is of one taste — liberation — though beings receive it by their capacity. The Sanskrit adds the physician who cures a man born blind with four herbs, which are emptiness, the signless, the wishless and the door of nirvāṇa.

The chapter tells the past of the buddha Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū and his sixteen sons, one of whom was Śākyamuni.

paraphrase: The parable of the jewel in the robe: a friend sews a priceless jewel into the robe of a man who is drunk and asleep; the man wanders in poverty until the friend shows him the jewel. So the disciples, content with small nirvāṇa, did not know they had long had the aspiration to all-knowledge.
